From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

## Threshold point: "FINAL, not to be re-opened"

The Seller's preamble says these positions were "settled at principal level" and are "FINAL". **Do not accept this on the Seller's say-so.** It is an assertion in the counterparty's covering note, and nothing in the package evidences it. Several "settled" positions are also contradicted by the Seller's own Disclosure Letter (see Bluefen, Riverlark and Ironquay below).

**Action:** Confirm directly with Wattlebridge's principals whether anything was agreed. If something was, get the exact terms in writing. Until then, treat every point as open.

The "market context" paragraph (caps of 10–20%, a 1% basket, 12–18 month limits, buyer-knowledge qualifiers) is the Seller's advocacy, not neutral evidence. Some figures are within a defensible range for *general* warranties. The real problem is that the Seller applies them to **everything**, including title, tax, fraud and known risks. That is not market.

---

## Part A: Liability architecture

Together, these provisions mean the Buyer would effectively have **no meaningful recourse for the issues already identified in due diligence.**

### 1. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3): highest priority
- It bars claims for anything the Buyer *or its advisers* knew, **"including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."** That is constructive knowledge of the entire data room.
- Combined with general disclosure, this wipes out warranty protection for every DD finding: Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar. The Seller has told us about these risks so that we cannot claim for them.
- **Push back:**
  - Delete the clause.
  - Replace it with an express provision that Buyer knowledge (actual, constructive or imputed) does not limit claims.
  - Fallback: actual knowledge of named deal-team individuals of the specific breach only, and never applying to indemnities or fundamental or tax warranties.

### 2. General disclosure (Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2; Sched 7)
- Disclosing "every fact… in the data room", the Accounts, the registers and public records is unacceptable.
- **Push back:**
  - Only fair, specific disclosures qualify the warranties, with enough detail for the Buyer to identify the nature, scope and effect of the matter.
  - Data room documents count only where a specific disclosure refers to them.
  - Disclosures must not qualify title, capacity or tax warranties, or any indemnity.
- **Para 1.4 (non-admission):** acceptable as drafted, but it must not dilute warranty or indemnity scope.
- **Staleness:** the data room is fixed at 22 September 2026, six weeks ago. Require an updated data room index and a bring-down. Any disclosure made between signing and Completion must not cure a breach. Instead it should trigger Buyer rights: termination, an indemnity or a price adjustment.

### 3. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
- **Push back:** carve out fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct and wilful concealment by the Seller or its representatives from every limitation, the exclusive-remedy clause and the non-reliance clause.
- Note that non-reliance clauses do not reliably exclude liability for misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law. Still, we should not concede the point contractually.

### 4. Fundamental warranties at the general cap and time limit
- It is not credible to cap title and capacity at AUD 4.8m on a AUD 24m share purchase "for administrative simplicity". If title fails, we have bought nothing.
- **Push back:**
  - Title and capacity capped at 100% of the price.
  - No de minimis or basket.
  - Not subject to disclosure.
  - Claim period of at least 6–7 years, or the statutory limitation period, with the SPA executed as a deed.

### 5. "Limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13)
This default rule would quietly apply the 18-month limit, AUD 4.8m cap and basket to the tax indemnity, specific indemnities and fundamental warranties. **Reverse it.** Each limitation should apply only to general warranty claims, and the carve-outs should be listed expressly.

### 6. Cap: 20% (AUD 4.8m) for general warranties
- This is within range for general warranties only, and only if the carve-outs above and below are secured.
- Consider W&I insurance as an alternative structure.
- **Recovery risk:** Harbourglass is a venture vehicle and may distribute sale proceeds quickly. Seek an **escrow or retention** (for example 10–15% for 18 months, plus a separate escrow for the specific indemnities), or a parent or fund guarantee.

### 7. Thresholds: AUD 25k de minimis and AUD 250k basket, recovering only the excess
- The basket is about 1.04% of price. The "excess only" feature is the bigger problem.
- **Push back:**
  - A tipping basket, so the full amount is recoverable once the basket is exceeded.
  - De minimis around AUD 10k.
  - Related claims from the same facts aggregated for de minimis purposes.
  - Thresholds do not apply to tax, fundamental warranties or indemnities.

### 8. Time limits: 18 months for general warranties
- 18 months is acceptable for general warranties if it covers at least one full audit cycle.
- **Tax:** the tax warranties and indemnity must run longer. ATO amendment periods are typically up to 4 years for companies, and unlimited for fraud or evasion. Seek about 5–7 years, or the amendment period plus 3–6 months.

### 9. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Reject.** We need a standalone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax. It should be:
  - free of the de minimis and basket,
  - capped at the price,
  - long-dated,
  - not qualified by disclosure,
  - supported by conduct-of-claims provisions.
- For a SaaS target, IP is core value. Seek a longer IP warranty period (for example 3 years) and a higher cap. In any event, the Ironquay matter needs its own indemnity (item 13).

---

## Part B: Specific transaction issues

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter repeatedly contradicts its "Update". Use that inconsistency in negotiation.

### 10. Bluefen: about AUD 3.6m revenue, around 30% of FY26
- **Update says:** "addressed"; reasonable endeavours; treated as satisfied once written consent is delivered.
- **Disclosure Letter para 2 says:** no final consent, and no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
- **The risk:** a consent that comes with adverse conditions (repricing, new termination rights, security) would technically satisfy the Seller's drafting.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a condition precedent, waivable **only by the Buyer**.
  - The consent must be unconditional, or on conditions acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably.
  - All cl 11.3 conditions must be satisfied, with no amendment to contract terms.
  - The Seller should use "all reasonable endeavours", with Buyer involvement in communications with Bluefen.
  - Include a longstop date and a Buyer termination right.
  - Consider a price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or materially changes terms within, say, 12 months.

### 11. Riverlark: about AUD 3.2m facility outstanding
- **Seller proposes:** release "following Completion".
- **The problem:** this is incompatible with debt-free/cash-free. We would pay the full price while the Company stays encumbered and the change-control clause (cl 8.1) may trigger a default.
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion, require a payoff letter stating the exact payout figure and committing to release on receipt.
  - The payout is paid at Completion directly from the price and deducted as Debt.
  - At Completion, deliver an executed deed of release and PPSR financing change statements, or an irrevocable undertaking to lodge them within 1–2 business days.
  - Include an indemnity for any residual liability.

### 12. Employee Completion bonuses: AUD 420,000 (DD-005)
- **Seller proposes:** "a matter for the Seller" but not itemised in the funds flow.
- **The risk:** in practice the Company pays them, possibly after Completion because of the continued-employment conditions. That is value leaking to the Buyer's cost. The disclosure also does not address PAYG withholding, payroll tax, superannuation (to be confirmed) or other on-costs.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the full amount, plus all on-costs, as Debt or Transaction Costs deducted from the price, or paid through payroll at Completion from Seller proceeds.
  - Include an uncapped indemnity for any shortfall.
  - Obtain copies of all bonus letters and confirm there are no further arrangements.

### 13. Ironquay IP / SOW3 (DD-004 cl 7.3, DD-010)
- **Why it matters:** title to the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, and there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment. The Company may not own core IP.
- **Seller proposes:** indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment. That is inadequate, because it covers the fee but not the loss of the IP.
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion, provide evidence of payment, or pay the AUD 180k at Completion and deduct it from the price.
  - A **confirmatory IP assignment deed executed by Ironquay** as a condition precedent or Completion deliverable.
  - A broader specific indemnity covering third-party IP claims, re-licensing and re-engineering costs, and loss of use. It should sit outside the cap, basket and time limits and be unaffected by disclosure or knowledge.

### 14. DD-006 data export incident
- **Seller says:** "Preliminary… not expected to be material". This is unsupported.
- **The facts disclosed:**
  - A download link was sent to an unintended external address.
  - About 1,240 records were potentially exposed: names, business emails, roles and timestamps.
  - Access, scope and notification obligations are not yet established.
- **The regulatory issue:** under the Privacy Act's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days of becoming aware of a suspected eligible data breach. The incident predates 22 September and it is now 4 November, so ask immediately whether the assessment was completed and what it concluded. Penalty exposure has risen materially since the 2022 amendments.
- **Contractual exposure:** customer contracts, possibly including Bluefen, may impose their own notification duties.
- **Push back:**
  - Require the forensic or incident report, the NDB assessment, and copies of any notifications to the OAIC, affected individuals or customers.
  - Include a **specific indemnity** outside the cap, basket and time limits, covering regulatory penalties, notification and remediation costs, third-party and customer claims, and credits.
  - Add warranties on privacy compliance and that no other incidents have occurred.
  - Add interim covenants requiring Buyer consultation on handling the incident.
  - Consider a Buyer termination right or a price adjustment if the investigation confirms an eligible breach.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals: 3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k (DD-008, DD-011)
- **Seller says:** "ordinary-course operating costs".
- **Why it is not that simple:** the Disclosure Letter itself says the renewals are related and should be read together, and does not say they are ordinary course, terminable or accrued. Three identical related contracts can indicate splitting to stay under an approval or conduct-of-business threshold.
- **Push back:**
  - Obtain the contracts and confirm when they were signed, their term, termination rights and business rationale.
  - If they were entered in the interim period or are not genuinely needed, require Buyer consent, termination before Completion, or treatment of the committed spend as Debt or Leakage.
  - Strengthen the conduct-of-business covenant so that related commitments aggregate against the threshold.

### 16. Title (DD-012 share register)
- **Seller relies on:** the register alone. A register is only prima facie evidence, and the Seller itself notes the Buyer has not verified title.
- **Push back:**
  - Run ASIC company searches and PPSR searches against both the Seller and the Company.
  - Obtain the constitution and any shareholder agreement, with pre-emption waivers.
  - Obtain confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or employee equity, given the target is venture-backed.
  - Require share certificates (or a lost-certificate indemnity) and releases of any share security.
  - Title warranty treated as fundamental, as in item 4.

### 17. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower priority
- **Office lease:** a notification obligation applies. Make the notice a Completion deliverable.
- **Mossvale:** the Seller says the restriction is on assignment only. Verify the full clause and its definitions (for example "assignment" deemed to include change in control), and verify this for the lease too.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright**
1. The "FINAL / not re-opened" framing. Verify with principals.
2. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3). Replace it with a provision that Buyer knowledge does not limit claims.
3. General data room and public-record disclosure. Allow specific, fair disclosure only, and require an updated bring-down.
4. The "all Claims" application of limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Carve out fraud and wilful concealment.
5. Fundamental warranties at the general cap. Title and capacity should be capped at 100% of price, with a 6–7 year period and no thresholds.
6. Tax and IP folded into the general regime. Require a standalone tax indemnity and an enhanced IP regime.

**Restructure deal-specific risks** (as conditions, Completion deliverables, price deductions or specific indemnities, not warranties)
7. **Bluefen:** Buyer-only waivable condition precedent; unconditional consent; all reasonable endeavours; longstop date.
8. **Riverlark:** payoff letter, payment from the price at Completion, deed of release and PPSR discharges at Completion.
9. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus on-costs deducted as Debt or Transaction Costs, with an indemnity.
10. **Ironquay:** payment or deduction of the AUD 180k, an executed confirmatory assignment, and a broad IP indemnity.
11. **DD-006:** urgent disclosure of the NDB assessment and forensic findings, a specific privacy indemnity, and termination or price rights.
12. **Sandbar:** diligence the contracts; treat as Debt or Leakage, or require termination, if not genuinely ordinary course.
13. **Title:** independent searches and capitalisation confirmations.

**Negotiable** (reasonable trade-offs, provided the above is secured)
14. General cap of 20% (or W&I insurance), an 18-month general claims period, a tipping basket, de minimis around AUD 10k with related claims aggregated, and escrow or a guarantee to secure recovery from a fund seller.

**Immediate information requests:** Bluefen consent status and cl 11.3 conditions; Riverlark payout figure; bonus letters; Ironquay payment evidence; DD-006 forensic report and NDB assessment; Sandbar contracts; capitalisation table and searches; full DD-007 and DD-009 clauses.

*This analysis is based only on the Seller's summary and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying DD documents or full SPA text. Statutory points (Privacy Act, ATO amendment periods, limitation periods) should be confirmed by Wattlebridge's NSW counsel before the mark-up is issued.*

- **The regulatory issue:** under the Privacy Act's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days of becoming aware of a suspected eligible data breach. The incident predates 22 September and it is now 4 November, so ask immediately whether the assessment was completed and what it concluded. Penalty exposure has risen materially since the 2022 amendments.
- **Contractual exposure:** customer contracts, possibly including Bluefen, may impose their own notification duties.
- **Push back:**
  - Require the forensic or incident report, the NDB assessment, and copies of any notifications to the OAIC, affected individuals or customers.
  - Include a **specific indemnity** outside the cap, basket and time limits, covering regulatory penalties, notification and remediation costs, third-party and customer claims, and credits.
  - Add warranties on privacy compliance and that no other incidents have occurred.
  - Add interim covenants requiring Buyer consultation on handling the incident.
  - Consider a Buyer termination right or a price adjustment if the investigation confirms an eligible breach.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals: 3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k (DD-008, DD-011)
- **Seller says:** "ordinary-course operating costs".
- **Why it is not that simple:** the Disclosure Letter itself says the renewals are related and should be read together, and does not say they are ordinary course, terminable or accrued. Three identical related contracts can indicate splitting to stay under an approval or conduct-of-business threshold.
- **Push back:**
  - Obtain the contracts and confirm when they were signed, their term, termination rights and business rationale.
  - If they were entered in the interim period or are not genuinely needed, require Buyer consent, termination before Completion, or treatment of the committed spend as Debt or Leakage.
  - Strengthen the conduct-of-business covenant so that related commitments aggregate against the threshold.

### 16. Title (DD-012 share register)
- **Seller relies on:** the register alone. A register is only prima facie evidence, and the Seller itself notes the Buyer has not verified title.
- **Push back:**
  - Run ASIC company searches and PPSR searches against both the Seller and the Company.
  - Obtain the constitution and any shareholder agreement, with pre-emption waivers.
  - Obtain confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or employee equity, given the target is venture-backed.
  - Require share certificates (or a lost-certificate indemnity) and releases of any share security.
  - Title warranty treated as fundamental, as in item 4.

### 17. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower priority
- **Office lease:** a notification obligation applies. Make the notice a Completion deliverable.
- **Mossvale:** the Seller says the restriction is on assignment only. Verify the full clause and its definitions (for example "assignment" deemed to include change in control), and verify this for the lease too.

## Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright**
1. The "FINAL / not re-opened" framing. Verify with principals.
2. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3). Replace it with a provision that Buyer knowledge does not limit claims.
3. General data room and public-record disclosure. Allow specific, fair disclosure only, and require an updated bring-down.
4. The "all Claims" application of limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Carve out fraud and wilful concealment.
5. Fundamental warranties at the general cap. Title and capacity should be capped at 100% of price, with a 6–7 year period and no thresholds.
6. Tax and IP folded into the general regime. Require a standalone tax indemnity and an enhanced IP regime.

**Restructure deal-specific risks** (as conditions, Completion deliverables, price deductions or specific indemnities, not warranties)
7. **Bluefen:** Buyer-only waivable condition precedent; unconditional consent; all reasonable endeavours; longstop date.
8. **Riverlark:** payoff letter, payment from the price at Completion, deed of release and PPSR discharges at Completion.
9. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus on-costs deducted as Debt or Transaction Costs, with an indemnity.
10. **Ironquay:** payment or deduction of the AUD 180k, an executed confirmatory assignment, and a broad IP indemnity.
11. **DD-006:** urgent disclosure of the NDB assessment and forensic findings, a specific privacy indemnity, and termination or price rights.
12. **Sandbar:** diligence the contracts; treat as Debt or Leakage, or require termination, if not genuinely ordinary course.
13. **Title:** independent searches and capitalisation confirmations.

**Negotiable** (reasonable trade-offs, provided the above is secured)
14. General cap of 20% (or W&I insurance), an 18-month general claims period, a tipping basket, de minimis around AUD 10k with related claims aggregated, and escrow or a guarantee to secure recovery from a fund seller.

**Immediate information requests:** Bluefen consent status and cl 11.3 conditions; Riverlark payout figure; bonus letters; Ironquay payment evidence; DD-006 forensic report and NDB assessment; Sandbar contracts; capitalisation table and searches; full DD-007 and DD-009 clauses.
